10.0.s.en: 1. A warning against a little folly:

10.0.0.en: 1 Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour and ferment: a little folly is weightier than wisdom and honour. 2 A wise man's heart is at his right hand; but a fool's heart at his left. 3 Yea also, when he that is a fool walketh by the way, his wisdom faileth him, and he saith to every one that he is a fool.

10.0.1.en: "Dead flies cause the ointment of the apothecary to send forth a stinking savour and ferment:

10.0.2.en: a little folly is weightier than wisdom and honour" [1].

10.0.3.en: The perfumer spends every effort to offer a precious perfume, but if a small fly falls into it, it stinks and ferments and spoils all the labor and the materials he used. So every laxity toward folly, however trivial it may seem, destroys what the spiritual man has gained of wisdom and spiritual honor through hard striving.

10.0.4.en: * When the wretched man is troubled by flies he himself becomes a fly, belonging to Satan. It is said that "Beelzebub" really means "prince of flies" or "king of flies" [whoever worships him becomes a fly].

10.0.5.en: St. Augustine * Beware of trifling matters lest you fall into their great ones. Do not be slack in your work, lest you be put to shame when you are found among your companions.

10.0.6.en: St. Isaac the Syrian Life in Christ Jesus our Lord, or the wise spiritual life, is a perfume that spreads to fill the whole house with the sweet fragrance of Christ, yet making light of what we think to be trivial small matters ruins our life and makes us like flies. Therefore the Preacher reveals to us a spiritual line of defense, saying:

10.1.0.en: "A wise man's heart is at his right hand; but a fool's heart at his left" [2].

10.1.1.en: The first sets his heart on goodness, or on the Kingdom of God, to enjoy the right hand of God, while the second has all his energies absorbed in evil, in the kingdom of darkness, so his lot is with those of the left. In other words, the right hand signifies concern for heavenly things, while the left signifies entanglement in temporal things.

10.2.0.en: "Yea also, when he that is a fool walketh by the way, his wisdom faileth him, and he saith to every one that he is a fool" [3].

10.2.1.en: The fool practices his folly all along the way, at every opportunity, wherever he is found, without restraint... and without occasion "he saith to every one that he is a fool," declaring his folly without shame or modesty... as though folly had become his nature, which he cannot hide.

10.2.2.en: The fool, without heavenly wisdom, does not grow wiser with the days, but with time loses even natural understanding, "for unto every one that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance: but from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath" (Mt 25:29).

10.3.s.en: 2. A warning against confronting injustice with violence:

10.3.0.en: 4 If the spirit of the ruler rise up against thee, leave not thy place; for yielding pacifieth great offences. 5 There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, as an error which proceedeth from the ruler: 6 Folly is set in great dignity, and the rich sit in low place. 7 I have seen servants upon horses, and princes walking as servants upon the earth. 8 He that diggeth a pit shall fall into it; and whoso breaketh an hedge, a serpent shall bite him. 9 Whoso removeth stones shall be hurt therewith; and he that cleaveth wood shall be endangered thereby. 10 If the iron be blunt, and he do not whet the edge, then must he put to more strength: but wisdom is profitable to prosper.

10.3.1.en: Some see that the wise Solomon here guides the people to walk in a spirit of submission to those in authority, perhaps because some of the rich had rebelled against him on account of the increase of taxes owing to his many projects, and had threatened disobedience and revolt.

10.4.s.en: a. Quarreling with rulers is not fitting:

10.4.0.en: "If the spirit of the ruler rise up against thee, leave not thy place; for yielding pacifieth great offences" [4].

10.4.1.en: If the governor or the king is angry with you because of a slander that reached him, do not leave your place, that is, do not abandon your national role. Be calm. Do not rebel against him but wait quietly, practicing positive work, and you will win him for yourself and for others!

10.5.0.en: The wise Solomon regards it as a grievous thing that happens under the sun that the base occupy some positions of leadership while the wise, the understanding and the faithful are left behind. Some fools occupy the highest posts and lofty offices while the wise are left in lowly positions. He saw servants upon horses and princes walking as servants upon the earth [7], meaning that those without knowledge or experience have occupied leading positions, walking in displays of grandeur and pomp, while those of rare competence are despised.

10.5.1.en: The wise Solomon saw all this "under the sun" [5], where injustice and disorder often rule human life through the ages, but in the other life, where there is no need of the sun (Rev 21:23), justice, love and holiness reign!

10.5.2.en: St. Jerome sees that the spirit of the ruler here [4] refers to the devil, who does not cease attacking the children of God, those who by the quiet Spirit of the Lord Christ shatter his plans and snares, and close the doors of their hearts in his face, shattering his domination and violence.

10.5.3.en: * Why do you shut the doors of your heart in the face of the Bridegroom? Open them to Christ and close them before Satan, as in the saying: "If the spirit of the ruler rise up against thee, leave not thy place."

10.5.4.en: St. Jerome He also speaks of the spirit of the ruler as a symbol of sin, which must be met with the quiet Spirit of Christ.

10.5.5.en: * Let us return first to the text quoted: "If the spirit of the ruler rise up against thee, leave not thy place." This phrase is followed by the words: "for yielding pacifieth great offences," that is, if the serpent finds its way into your thoughts you must keep your heart with all diligence, singing with David: "Cleanse thou me from secret faults. Keep back thy servant also from presumptuous sins," and so you do not slip into the great transgression, that is, falling into sin in deed.

10.6.0.en: The wise Solomon offers a common counsel to the unjust among those in authority and to the people, asking the unjust to cease from his injustice because what they practice against others comes upon him, and calming the fears of the oppressed, who must keep within their limits, not out of surrender and weakness, but out of faith in the justice of God, who permits him who fills a cup for his brethren to drink from it himself: "He that diggeth a pit shall fall into it; and whoso breaketh an hedge, a serpent shall bite him" [8].

10.6.1.en: Haman prepared a gallows for Mordecai and was hanged on it (Esth 7:10), and the inventor of the Guillotine, which bore his name, was executed by it... But what is greater, the Cross by which the devil thought to destroy the Lord Christ and blot out His name, behold it destroys the powers of Satan and scatters his authority over the believers.

10.6.2.en: Whoever breaks down a hedge behind which a believer shelters is bitten by a serpent hiding in it, for serpents often take shelter in old ruins or an old crevice. In other words, whoever is intent on tearing down the walls of others instead of working constructively in his own life or the life of others, the serpent of envy and hatred bites him, and he dies and perishes eternally.

10.6.3.en: * He who scatters the safety of others falls by the bite of the serpent.

10.6.4.en: St. Gregory the Wonderworker The Preacher continues his discourse, saying:

10.6.5.en: "Whoso removeth stones shall be hurt therewith; and he that cleaveth wood shall be endangered thereby.

10.7.0.en: If the iron be blunt, and he do not whet the edge, then must he put to more strength" [9-10].

10.7.1.en: He who removes stones in order to bring down a building has a stone fall on his head and is hurt, and then he regrets what he did, wishing he had left the stones in the building without pulling them out. Perhaps by this he means that he who opposes those in authority with the aim of reform, by biting criticism, loses much himself while he shakes others.

10.7.2.en: Likewise, he who cleaves wood with a blunt iron tool is forced to strike with force and risks the head of the tool flying off and striking him.

10.8.0.en: In all the preceding examples the Preacher affirms that the reform of rulers is not achieved by violence and biting criticism but by a spirit of meekness and love, with reliance on the work of God and faith in His justice... This is the wisdom of which he says: "But wisdom is profitable to prosper" [10], that is, by quiet wisdom our guidance of those in authority and of our own lives succeeds. Wisdom shatters the pride of the unjust and gives those who practice it the ability to work in a spirit of sincere obedience.

10.9.s.en: 3. A warning against the evil tongue:

10.9.0.en: 11 If the serpent bite without enchantment, there is no profit to the enchanter. 12 The words of a wise man's mouth are gracious; but the lips of a fool will swallow up himself. 13 The beginning of the words of his mouth is foolishness: and the end of his talk is mischievous madness. 14 A fool also is full of words: a man cannot tell what shall be; and what shall be after him, who can tell him? 15 The labour of the foolish wearieth every one of them, because he knoweth not how to go to the city.

10.9.1.en: Having called those in authority and those under them to a spirit of quiet wisdom that gives success to both parties, the Preacher translates this wisdom practically by warning against the evil tongue as against the bites of the deadly serpent, asking us to have the anointing of grace on our lips so that we do not speak foolishly.

10.9.2.en: "If the serpent bite without enchantment, there is no profit to the enchanter (so the one of evil tongue does no better than it)" [11].

10.9.3.en: If the rebel is like a serpent that bites, let us enchant him with meekness and wise love before he bites us, as Jacob did when he offered a gift to Esau in a spirit of humility (Gen 32:13-21), and as Abigail did with David in his rage against Nabal her husband (1 Sam 25:18-35).

10.10.0.en: The wise man meets the rage of others with a spirit of meekness and grace, but the fool's mouth drives him into folly and madness... He multiplies words without realizing the consequences [14], so he falls into weariness, that is, his strength fails, and he loses the ability to know the way by which he enters the city. In other words, violent words make man lose wisdom, even natural wisdom, as well as strength and knowledge, and he remains as one outside the city of God!

10.10.1.en: To this day some villagers are accustomed to call one who specializes in bringing serpents out of their holes; when they see a serpent enter a hole they summon him, and he sings and beats on the pipe or the drum until the serpent comes out and dances to the tones of the song, and then he pulls out its teeth... Then it is unable to bite even a small child (Ps 58:4-5). So if you enchant the violent man with all wisdom full of sweetness, in a spirit of sincere submission in the Lord, you shatter the fangs of his evil before he kills you. But if you let him bite you, enchantment does not help once his venom has spread through your body.

10.10.2.en: Abba Moses, in his conferences with St. John Cassian, sees that the enchantment here is the confession and disclosure of sins, for it shatters the power of the living devil and removes from us the deadly venom of sin. He says: [The bite of a serpent without an enchanter present is dangerous, that is, the danger is that no suggestion or thought arising from Satan be disclosed to the enchanter in confession. By the enchanter I mean the company of spiritual men who know how to treat wounds with the words of Holy Scripture, and draw the deadly venom of the viper from the heart].

10.10.3.en: * If the serpent - Satan - secretly bites a person, it afflicts that person with the venom of sin. And if the afflicted one remains silent and does not repent and does not want to confess his wound to his brother and his master, then his brother and master, who have his cure, cannot help him well, for if the patient is ashamed to confess his wound to the physician, the medicine does not heal him...

10.10.4.en: St. Jerome The wise Solomon compares the words of the wise man with the words of the fool thus:

10.10.5.en: a. The words of the wise man reveal the grace of love, calm and wisdom in his heart, while the words of the fool reveal the corruption of his heart, so they expose him to mockery and ridicule and even destruction: "The words of a wise man's mouth are gracious; but the lips of a fool will swallow up himself" [12]. The Lord Christ says: "For by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned" (Mt 12:37), and the Psalmist says: "So they shall make their own tongue to fall upon themselves" (Ps 64:8). And as Solomon said of Adonijah, who asked for his father's wife to be his wife: "Adonijah hath spoken this word against himself" (1 Kgs 2:32).

10.10.6.en: b. The fool begins his words by revealing the folly of his heart, which is his evil spring, and his corrupt treasure that brings forth foolishness; this spring gradually bursts forth through the fool's rashness in his words until it sends out fiery missiles and turns him into a state near to madness, so that no one can control his tongue or master his words: "The beginning of the words of his mouth is foolishness: and the end of his talk is mischievous madness" [13].

10.10.7.en: c. The fool repeats his idle words and thinks that by this he prevails, but in reality he loses the battle during his life and even after his death, for the traces of his evil words keep pursuing him even after death. "A fool also is full of words: a man cannot tell what shall be; and what shall be after him, who can tell him?" [14].

10.11.0.en: d. Since the fool speaks with rage and without stopping, he not only loses the battle - that is, loses his right - but falls into weariness because of his psychological fatigue and his sense of failure and injustice: "The labour of the foolish wearieth every one of them" [15].

10.11.1.en: e. The Preacher ends his discourse here by saying of the fool who is proud in his folly: "because he knoweth not how to go to the city" [15], that is, he loses the ability even to perceive how to enter the city, which is something no man is ignorant of. And Abba Abraham says in his conference with St. John Cassian: [And so, since they stray from the royal heavenly way, they are unable to reach the city toward which our gaze has been directed. The book of Ecclesiastes expressed it symbolically, saying of it that it is Jerusalem... that is, the Jerusalem above, which is the mother of us all (Gal 4:26).

10.12.0.en: "Woe to thee, O land, when thy king is a child, and thy princes eat in the morning!

10.12.1.en: Blessed art thou, O land, when thy king is the son of nobles, and thy princes eat in due season, for strength, and not for drunkenness!" [16-17].

10.12.2.en: Let us beware lest our king, "our inner man," be a child, that is, immature in heavenly wisdom, and care for temporal pleasures like eating in the morning instead of earnest work, and forget that he is noble (a son of God and a temple of the Holy Spirit), and that he should use the world to work with strength and not for pleasure and drunkenness with temporal things.

10.12.3.en: What is this land but our body, which falls under woe and curse if a soul dwells in it that is neither wise nor mature, seeking a life of amusement and license, so that our body brings forth for us the thorns of sin and the thistles of defilement, and is good for nothing... It wants to eat and drink and amuse itself without order or purpose. But the same body, if it is sanctified with the soul that enjoys the honor of Christ and is counted a queen (Rev 1:6), knows how to strive, turning the body into the garden of God bearing the fruit of the Spirit.

10.12.4.en: St. Augustine sees that the first land signifies the city of the devil and the other the city of God, for he says:

10.12.5.en: [I think it more fitting for us to quote from this book what concerns the two cities, one of Satan and the other the city of Christ, and what concerns their two kings: "Satan and Christ."]

10.12.6.en: The Preacher says: "Woe to thee, O land, when thy king is a child, and thy princes eat in the morning!" "Blessed art thou, O land, when thy king is the son of nobles, and thy princes eat in due season, for strength, and not for drunkenness (disorder)."

10.12.7.en: He calls Satan a child because of his folly, his pride, his rashness, his lack of skill in management and the rest of the vices for which this age is known; but Christ is the son of nobles - the free - that is, the holy patriarchs (fathers), who belong to the free city, for He was born of them according to the flesh. The princes of the other cities eat in the morning, that is, before the proper time, because they do not expect the joy that comes in its true time alone, that is, in the age to come, desiring to become happy quickly through the fame of this present world, but the princes of the city of Christ wait patiently for the time of the blessing that does not pass away.

10.13.0.en: "By much slothfulness the building decayeth (falls apart); and through idleness of the hands the house droppeth through. A feast is made for laughter, and wine maketh merry the living: but money answereth all things." [18-19].

10.13.1.en: Through sloth and neglect man inclines to rest, not caring even for the upkeep of his house; damage may come to the roof and woodworm eat its timbers, and man remains in his sloth until the roof falls and he finds no shelter. The roof signifies the living spiritual building, for Peter went up on the housetop to pray and saw a heavenly vision (Acts 10:9-16). Through sloth we come down from the housetop, where the heavenly vision is, to being occupied with dust.

10.13.2.en: St. Isaac the Syrian urges us to leave sloth and strive in watchfulness, saying: [The soul that practices works of vigil and excels in them has in its will the two eyes of the Cherubim, by which it sees at all times the heavenly visions and draws near to them].

10.13.3.en: Through sloth the hands lose their ability to work and hang down in slackness.

10.13.4.en: Through sloth the house droppeth through, that is, it cracks and collapses... It is a painful sight for a man to see the roof of his house collapsing and to stand with folded hands, not moving to repair it, until the whole house collapses!

10.13.5.en: In the spiritual sense, through sloth man loses the heavenly spiritual vision because the roof of his soul falls apart, and his hands are unable to do spiritual work, and his inner man collapses.

10.13.6.en: While sloth makes man lose his ability for earnest constructive work, so that he feels that everything in him has collapsed and that he is in a state of utter helplessness, behold in a life of amusement he is exceedingly active. He makes feasts for laughter and spends his life in drunkenness, saying that he has much silver by which he can obtain all he desires. In this he cannot experience the words of our teacher the Apostle Peter: "Pass the time of your sojourning here in fear: forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers; but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot" (1 Pet 1:17-19).

10.14.0.en: "Curse not the king, no not in thy thought; and curse not the rich in thy bedchamber: for a bird of the air shall carry the voice, and that which hath wings shall tell the matter." [20].

10.14.1.en: Every sin begins in thought, so it must be pursued at its beginning... It is not fitting for us, as those who belong to God, to curse anyone, especially those in authority... and let us realize that what we do in secret is exposed openly. Perhaps by the bird of the air he meant spies and informers! Let us be faithful in our depths so that we fear no one. As the Apostle Paul says: "Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power? do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same" (Rom 13:3).

10.14.2.en: Let our inside be like our outside, pure, insulting no one, so that we may be filled with the surpassing peace of God.

10.14.3.en: Thus, as the wise Solomon calls us to true wisdom, he warns us of the negative side of falling into what we call trivial matters or small sins, and urges us not to confront the injustice of officials with violence, trusting in God's work with us and with them and His care and concern for us; he also warned us of the evil tongue as of madness, and asked us not to live as child kings but as noble kings and wise in the Lord, and asks us not to walk in slackness and sloth, and finally not to curse anyone even in our hidden hearts.
